Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the people of Israel were property that Yahweh received as **his inheritance**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the tribe that belongs to him]
See how you translated this expression in 31:35.

20.q: מַפֵּץ־אַתָּ֣ה לִ֔⁠י כְּלֵ֖י מִלְחָמָ֑ה וְ⁠נִפַּצְתִּ֤י בְ⁠ךָ֙ גּוֹיִ֔ם וְ⁠הִשְׁחַתִּ֥י בְ⁠ךָ֖ מַמְלָכֽוֹת
20.note: From here through verse 23 Yahweh speaks to the nation of Babylon, which he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he controls Babylon. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Babylon. Alternate translation: [Babylon is a shatterer for me, weapons of war, and with it I have shattered nations, and with it I have destroyed kingdoms]

20.q: וְ⁠נִפַּצְתִּ֤י בְ⁠ךָ֙ גּוֹיִ֔ם וְ⁠הִשְׁחַתִּ֥י בְ⁠ךָ֖ מַמְלָכֽוֹת
20.note: From here through verse 23 Yahweh uses a repetitive series of clauses to communicate that what he is saying should be understood as comprehensive and overwhelming. Use a form in your language that someone would use to describe a situation that is comprehensive and overwhelming.

The pronoun **You** refers to a nation that Yahweh uses as his weapon in battle. This could mean: (1) Babylon, which Yahweh used to destroy other nations or (2) the army of the Medes, whom Yahweh will use to destroy Babylon. Alternate translation: [You, Babylon, are a shatterer for me]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the nation that he addresses were **a shatterer**, which would be a heavy club that a soldier swings in battle, and other **weapons of war**. This means that he uses that nation to fight battles. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You are one who destroys for me, one who fights my battles]

21.q: וְ⁠נִפַּצְתִּ֣י בְ⁠ךָ֔ ס֖וּס וְ⁠רֹֽכְב֑⁠וֹ וְ⁠נִפַּצְתִּ֣י בְ⁠ךָ֔ רֶ֖כֶב וְ⁠רֹכְבֽ⁠וֹ
21.note: Yahweh is not referring to a specific **horse**, **rider**, or **chariot**. He means these things in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And with you I have shattered many horses and their riders, and with you I have shattered many chariots and their riders]

22.q: וְ⁠נִפַּצְתִּ֤י בְ⁠ךָ֙ אִ֣ישׁ וְ⁠אִשָּׁ֔ה וְ⁠נִפַּצְתִּ֥י בְ⁠ךָ֖ זָקֵ֣ן וָ⁠נָ֑עַר וְ⁠נִפַּצְתִּ֣י בְ⁠ךָ֔ בָּח֖וּר וּ⁠בְתוּלָֽה
22.note: Yahweh is not referring to a specific **man**, **woman**, **old man**, **youth**, **young man**, or **virgin**. He means these kinds of people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And with you I have shattered many men and women, and with you I have shattered many old men and youths, and with you I have shattered many young men and virgins]

22.q: וְ⁠נִפַּצְתִּ֤י בְ⁠ךָ֙ אִ֣ישׁ וְ⁠אִשָּׁ֔ה וְ⁠נִפַּצְתִּ֥י בְ⁠ךָ֖ זָקֵ֣ן וָ⁠נָ֑עַר וְ⁠נִפַּצְתִּ֣י בְ⁠ךָ֔ בָּח֖וּר וּ⁠בְתוּלָֽה
22.note: Yahweh is referring to all of the people of the nations by naming pairs of opposites, **man and woman**, **old man and youth**, and **young man and virgin**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And with you I have shattered every kind of person, no matter their gender or age]

23.q: וְ⁠נִפַּצְתִּ֤י בְ⁠ךָ֙ רֹעֶ֣ה וְ⁠עֶדְר֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠נִפַּצְתִּ֥י בְ⁠ךָ֖ אִכָּ֣ר וְ⁠צִמְדּ֑⁠וֹ
23.note: Yahweh is not referring to a specific **shepherd**, **flock**, **plowman**, or **team**. He means these kinds of people and animals in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And with you I have shattered many shepherds and their flocks, and with you I have shattered many plowmen and their teams]

A **team** is a pair of animals such as oxen that a farmer yokes together to pull a plow. If your readers would not be familiar with what a team is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [and his plow animals]

The terms **governors** and **prefects** refer to officials who ruled provinces on behalf of a king. If your readers would not be familiar with what these officials did, you could use the names of similar officials that your readers would recognize, or you could use more general terms. This also occurs in verse 57. Alternate translation: [rulers and their officials]

24.note: In this verse Yahweh stops speaking to Babylon and instead speaks to the people of Israel in Zion, that is, Jerusalem. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use a natural way to mark that here Yahweh speaks to the Israelites. Alternate translation: [People of Israel, I want you to know that I will repay]

Here, **Babylon** represents “the people who live in Babylon.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And I will repay to the people of Babylon and to all the dwellers of Chaldea]

24.q: אֵ֧ת כָּל רָעָתָ֛⁠ם אֲשֶׁר עָשׂ֥וּ בְ⁠צִיּ֖וֹן
24.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [all that they wickedly did in Zion]

The pronoun **your** refers to the people of Israel, to whom Yahweh is speaking here. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [that they did in Zion before the eyes of you people of Israel]

Yahweh is using **to your eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “where you could see it.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [while you watched]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:8. This also occurs in verses 25, 26, 39, 48, 52, and 53.

25.q: הִנְ⁠נִ֨י אֵלֶ֜י⁠ךָ הַ֤ר הַ⁠מַּשְׁחִית֙ נְאֻם־יְהוָ֔ה הַ⁠מַּשְׁחִ֖ית אֶת־כָּל־הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ וְ⁠נָטִ֨יתִי אֶת־יָדִ֜⁠י עָלֶ֗י⁠ךָ וְ⁠גִלְגַּלְתִּ֨י⁠ךָ֙ מִן־הַ⁠סְּלָעִ֔ים וּ⁠נְתַתִּ֖י⁠ךָ לְ⁠הַ֥ר שְׂרֵפָֽה
25.note: From here through verse 26 Yahweh speaks to the nation of Babylon, which he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him what he intends to do to Babylon. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these verses as if he were speaking directly to the people about Babylon. Alternate translation: [Behold me, against Babylon, that mountain of destruction”—the declaration of Yahweh—“the one destroying all the earth. And I will stretch out my hand against it, and I will roll it from the cliffs, and I will make it into a mountain of burning]

In this verse and the next Yahweh stops speaking to the people of Israel and instead speaks to Babylon. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use a natural way to mark that here Yahweh begins speaking to Babylon. Alternate translation: [Babylon, behold me]
See how you translated the similar expression in 21:13.

Picturing Babylon as a **mountain of destruction** could mean: (1) that it is large, powerful, and unable to be conquered as it destroys other nations. Alternate translation: [destroying nation as impregnable as a mountain] (2) that it is like a mountain that is home to destroying bands of raiders who descend from there to destroy other nations. Alternate translation: [mountain home of raiders]

Yahweh says **all the earth** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [the one destroying nation after nation]
See how you translated the similar expression in 15:6.

25.q: וְ⁠גִלְגַּלְתִּ֨י⁠ךָ֙ מִן הַ⁠סְּלָעִ֔ים וּ⁠נְתַתִּ֖י⁠ךָ לְ⁠הַ֥ר שְׂרֵפָֽה
25.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the city of Babylon were on a mountain and he would roll it down **from the cliffs** and burn it until it was **a mountain of burning**. This means that he will destroy it completely. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will overthrow you completely, and I will leave you as nothing but burned ruins]

26.q: וְ⁠לֹֽא יִקְח֤וּ מִמְּ⁠ךָ֙ אֶ֣בֶן לְ⁠פִנָּ֔ה וְ⁠אֶ֖בֶן לְ⁠מֽוֹסָד֑וֹת
26.note: The implication is that Babylon will be ruined so completely that no one will even come there to gather building stones. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And no one will even come to your ruins to salvage a stone for a corner or a stone for foundations]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [nor will they take from you a stone for foundations]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **desolations** and **perpetuity**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [for you will remain desolate forever]

27.note: In verses 27 and 28 Jeremiah gives a series of commands to the nations around Babylon, even though he knows that they cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that these things must and will happen. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Babylon. Alternate translation: [To the nations around Babylon, I say, Lift up a banner]

The implication is that these armies are being set apart for a war that Yahweh himself has commanded, in the way that people set something apart for a holy purpose. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Set apart nations for Yahweh’s holy war against her]
The words **Ararat**, **Minni**, and **Ashkenaz** are the names of kingdoms that lay to the north of Babylon.

A **marshal** is a military officer who takes command of an army. If your readers would not be familiar with what a marshal is, you could use the name of a similar officer that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [a commander]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the bristling locust** comes in swarms that cover the whole land, so these **horses** would be too many to count. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Bring up horses that are as numerous as a swarm of locusts]

28.note: See how you translated this phrase in Jeremiah 51:27.

The pronoun **his** refers to each of the kings of Media whom Jeremiah mentions earlier in this verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and all the land that each of those kings rules]

29.note: From here through verse 32, Jeremiah talks about Babylon’s future defeat as though it had already happened. He, as God’s prophet, has already foreseen it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could continue to use a future tense for these events, as in the UST. Alternate translation: [And the land will quake and writhe]

Jeremiah is speaking of **the land** as if it were a living thing that could **writhe** in pain. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the land shook and trembled violently]

29.q: כִּ֣י קָ֤מָה עַל בָּבֶל֙ מַחְשְׁב֣וֹת יְהוָ֔ה
29.note: Jeremiah is using **the plans of Yahweh have stood** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh will certainly do what he has planned.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for Yahweh will surely carry out what he has planned against Babylon]

29.q: לָ⁠שׂ֞וּם אֶת אֶ֧רֶץ בָּבֶ֛ל לְ⁠שַׁמָּ֖ה מֵ⁠אֵ֥ין יוֹשֵֽׁב
29.note: Here, **to** marks **to make the land of Babylon a desolation, without a dweller** as the goal or purpose of **the plans of Yahweh** that he made **against Babylon**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

30.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [They have become as powerless as women] or [Their might has dried up, indeed, they have become as women]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the courage of the warriors of Babylon were water that **has dried up**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Their courage has failed completely]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **might**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [They have become powerless]

The point of this comparison is that just as **women** were weak and helpless before attacking soldiers, so the warriors of Babylon were weak and helpless. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [they have become feeble, unable to fight]

The pronoun **They** refers to the enemies who are attacking Babylon, not to the warriors of Babylon whom Jeremiah mentions earlier in this verse. The pronoun **her** refers to the city of Babylon. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The attackers have set Babylon’s dwellings on fire]

The expression **have been broken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they have broken her bars]

31.note: Jeremiah is not referring to a specific **runner**. He means messengers in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Messengers run to meet other messengers]

Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and an announcer runs to meet an announcer]

The expression **has been captured** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that enemies have seized his city from its end]

Jeremiah is using **from its end** as a common expression of the culture to mean “all of it.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from end to end] or [in its entirety]

32.note: The expression **have been seized** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the enemy has seized the fords]

The implication is that the enemies burned the reeds growing in **the marshes** so that no one from the city could hide there. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and they have burned the reeds in the marshes, so no one can hide there]

The expression **are terrified** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the men of war tremble in fear]

33.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 31:23.

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the city of Babylon were a young woman, calling it **Daughter Babylon**, which emphasizes its vulnerability. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Babylon] or [Poor Babylon]

The point of this comparison is that just as grain on **a threshing floor** is trampled and crushed, so the people of Babylon will be trampled in that city by their enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Babylon is like a threshing floor and its people are like the grain that will be crushed there at crushing time]

Yahweh is using **Yet a little while** as a common expression of the culture to mean “very soon.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Only a short time remains]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the time when he punishes Babylon were **the time of the harvest**, when farmers cut down the grain and thresh it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the time when I punish her will come]

34.note: Here the people of Jerusalem begin speaking. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that here in a natural way, as in the UST.

Here the people of Jerusalem are speaking as if Nebuchadnezzar were a beast that **has devoured** them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon has ruined us completely]

Here the people of Jerusalem are speaking as if they were fruit whose juice Nebuchadnezzar **has sucked** out. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he has taken everything from us]

Here the people of Jerusalem are speaking as if they were **an empty vessel** that Nebuchadnezzar drained and then set aside. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he has left us with nothing and cast us aside]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the sea monster** swallows its prey whole, so Nebuchadnezzar has taken away everything that the people of Jerusalem had. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [He has taken away everything we had, just as a sea monster swallows its prey whole]

A **sea monster** is a huge and frightening creature that people believed lived in the sea. If your readers would not be familiar with what a sea monster is, you could use the name of a similar creature that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [like a huge, frightening creature]

Here the people of Jerusalem are speaking as if the valuable things that Nebuchadnezzar took from them were **delicacies** with which he **filled his belly**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he has satisfied himself with my treasures]
The speaker says **my** here, but if this singular form of the pronoun would not be natural in your language, you could use the plural form in your translation. Alternate translation: [our]

Here the people of Jerusalem are speaking as if they were a dish that Nebuchadnezzar **has rinsed** out until nothing at all was left in it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he has left nothing at all of ours]

35.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **violence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [May Babylon be held responsible for violently harming me and my flesh]

The people of Zion are using this expression as a common expression of the culture to mean “May Babylon bear the guilt for the violence that its people did to us and to our relatives.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May Babylon be held guilty for the violence done to me and to my relatives]
Here, **my flesh** represents “my relatives.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and my relatives]
Jeremiah identifies the speaker only after the quotation. In your translation, you may want to identify the speaker before the quotation, as in the UST.

The people of Jerusalem are using this expression as a common expression of the culture to mean “May the people of Chaldea be held guilty for murdering our people.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And may the dwellers of Chaldea bear the guilt for shedding our blood]

Here, **Jerusalem** represents “the people who live in Jerusalem.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [say the people of Jerusalem]

36.note: See how you translated the same expression in 18:13.

The word translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [Because of this, Yahweh says]

36.q: רָב֙ אֶת רִיבֵ֔⁠ךְ וְ⁠נִקַּמְתִּ֖י אֶת נִקְמָתֵ֑⁠ךְ
36.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **contention** and **vengeance**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [ready to defend you, and I will repay those who wronged you]

36.q: רָב֙ אֶת רִיבֵ֔⁠ךְ וְ⁠נִקַּמְתִּ֖י אֶת נִקְמָתֵ֑⁠ךְ
36.note: This is poetic language. In the original language, the verb and the noun in each of these two phrases come from the same root. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here.

The pronoun **your** in this verse refers to the people of Jerusalem, also called Zion in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the contention of you people in Jerusalem]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the waters that supplied Babylon and the wealth that came with them were **her sea** and **her fountain**, which he will dry up. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will dry up the waters that supply her, and I will cut off the source of her wealth]
The pronoun **her** in this verse refers to Babylon. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and I will dry up Babylon’s sea]

37.note: The implication is that these **heaps** are piles of rubble that will be left after enemies destroy the city. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And Babylon will become heaps of rubble after her enemies destroy her]

37.q: מְעוֹן תַּנִּ֛ים שַׁמָּ֥ה וּ⁠שְׁרֵקָ֖ה מֵ⁠אֵ֥ין יוֹשֵֽׁב
37.note: Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [it will become a habitation of jackals, it will become a desolation and an object of hissing, and it will be without a dweller]

The word translated as **a hissing** refers to a whistling or hissing sound that a person would make to show that he dislikes something very much. The person is expressing rejection of what he is seeing, disassociating himself from it. This could be because: (1) it is a horrible sight, or to show mockery of it, or both. (2) it is a place where demons might be, and so the sound is meant to ward them off. Use a natural way to show this in your language. Alternate translation: [and something that people will spit at] or [and something that will make people shudder]
See how you translated the similar expression in 9:11.
See how you translated the similar expression in 19:8.

38.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the people of Babylon. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Together the Babylonians roar like young lions]

38.q: יַחְדָּ֖ו כַּ⁠כְּפִרִ֣ים יִשְׁאָ֑גוּ נָעֲר֖וּ כְּ⁠גוֹרֵ֥י אֲרָיֽוֹת
38.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Together like the young lions they fiercely roar and growl]

38.q: יַחְדָּ֖ו כַּ⁠כְּפִרִ֣ים יִשְׁאָ֑גוּ נָעֲר֖וּ כְּ⁠גוֹרֵ֥י אֲרָיֽוֹת
38.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the young lions** roar fiercely as they hunt for prey, so the people of Babylon act fiercely toward the people of other nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Together they are fierce toward people of other nations, as young lions are when hunting other animals; they are aggressive like the cubs of lions]

39.note: The pronoun **they** in this verse continues to refer to the people of Babylon. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [When the people of Babylon grow hot, I will set out their feast]
**When they grow hot** refers to becoming thirsty, which represents the Babylonians becoming greedy to exploit other nations. Alternate translation: [When they are excited with greed]

Here Yahweh is speaking of giving Babylon the riches of other nations as though it were a **feast**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will let them have their fill] or [I will give them what they desire]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if he would give the people of Babylon so much wine that he would **make them drunk** and helpless. It means that he will allow them to exploit other nations excessively and become complacent. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will let them become rich and self-satisfied]

Here, **so that** marks **they may exult and sleep a sleep of perpetuity and not wake up** as the goal or purpose of Yahweh setting out the feast and making the people of Babylon drunk. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

Yahweh is referring to dying in a polite way by using the phrase **sleep a sleep of perpetuity and not wake up**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. This also occurs in verse 57. Alternate translation: [and die forever]

This is poetic language. In the original language, the verb translated as **sleep** and the noun translated as **a sleep** come from the same root. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here.

40.q: אֽוֹרִידֵ֖⁠ם כְּ⁠כָרִ֣ים לִ⁠טְב֑וֹחַ כְּ⁠אֵילִ֖ים עִם עַתּוּדִֽים
40.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **lambs** are led away helplessly **to the slaughter**, so the people of Babylon will be killed without being able to resist. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I will bring them down to be killed, helpless as lambs, rams, and male goats that are led away to be slaughtered]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I will bring them down like rams with male goats to the slaughter]

41.note: Jeremiah is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of astonishment. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Alas! Sheshach has been captured]
The word **Sheshach** is a code name for the city of Babylon. See how you translated it in 25:26.

41.q: אֵ֚יךְ נִלְכְּדָ֣ה שֵׁשַׁ֔ךְ וַ⁠תִּתָּפֵ֖שׂ תְּהִלַּ֣ת כָּל־הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ
41.note: The expressions **has been captured** and **has been seized** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [How enemies have captured Sheshach, and how they have seized the praise of all the earth]

Here, **the praise of all the earth** represents “the city that everyone on the earth praised.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the city that everyone on the earth praised has been seized]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **desolation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a desolate place]

42.q: עָלָ֥ה עַל־בָּבֶ֖ל הַ⁠יָּ֑ם בַּ⁠הֲמ֥וֹן גַּלָּ֖י⁠ו נִכְסָֽתָה
42.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Roaring waves of the sea have overwhelmed Babylon]

42.q: עָלָ֥ה עַל בָּבֶ֖ל הַ⁠יָּ֑ם בַּ⁠הֲמ֥וֹן גַּלָּ֖י⁠ו נִכְסָֽתָה
42.note: Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the armies attacking Babylon were **The sea** flooding over the city. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Invading armies have overwhelmed Babylon; they cover her like crashing ocean waves]

The expression **she has been covered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the tumult of its waves has covered her]

The pronoun **she** refers to Babylon, and the pronoun **its** refers to the sea. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Babylon has been covered with the tumult of the sea’s waves]

43.note: Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [they have become a land of dryness and a desert plain]

The terms **a land of dryness** and **a desert plain** mean similar things. Jeremiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [a completely barren wasteland]

43.q: אֶ֗רֶץ לֹֽא יֵשֵׁ֤ב בָּ⁠הֵן֙ כָּל אִ֔ישׁ
43.note: The pronoun **them** refers back to the cities of Babylon that Jeremiah mentions at the beginning of this verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [a land whose cities no man dwells in]

43.q: אֶ֗רֶץ לֹֽא יֵשֵׁ֤ב בָּ⁠הֵן֙ כָּל אִ֔ישׁ וְ⁠לֹֽא יַעֲבֹ֥ר בָּ⁠הֵ֖ן בֶּן אָדָֽם
43.note: Here the masculine terms **man** and **son of man** have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [a land where no people dwell, and where no human being passes through]

44.note: Yahweh is using **I will visit upon** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will punish.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar expression in 21:14. Alternate translation: [And I will punish Bel in Babylon]
The word **Bel** is the name of a god whom the people of Babylon worshiped.

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the idol **Bel** had swallowed the things that the people of Babylon plundered from other nations and that he would now bring them back up **from his mouth**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will make him give back what he has taken]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **swallowing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what he has swallowed]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the crowds of people who came to worship Bel were water that would **stream** toward him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the nations will not come to him in great numbers anymore]

Jeremiah speaks of the **wall of Babylon** as **fallen** even though that will still happen in the future. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a future tense. Alternate translation: [Even the wall of Babylon will fall down]

45.note: The implication is that Yahweh’s people are to leave the city before he destroys it. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Go out from her midst, my people, before Yahweh destroys that city]
The pronoun **my** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [People that belong to me, Yahweh]

Yahweh is speaking to his people, but refers to each of their lives as **his life**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use “your” instead of “his.” Alternate translation: [and each of you save your life]
See how you translated the similar expression in 4:8.

46.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if courage were something in the **heart** that could **grow soft**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And lest you lose heart] or [And lest you lose courage]

Here, **lest** indicates that Yahweh does not want the following things to happen, and in verse 47 he gives the reason why his people should not let their **heart grow soft** or **fear**. Alternate translation: [I do not want your heart to grow soft or for you to fear]

The expression **is heard** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [at the report that people spread through the land]

46.q: וּ⁠בָ֧א בַ⁠שָּׁנָ֣ה הַ⁠שְּׁמוּעָ֗ה וְ⁠אַחֲרָ֤י⁠ו בַּ⁠שָּׁנָה֙ הַ⁠שְּׁמוּעָ֔ה
46.note: Yahweh is using this expression as a common expression of the culture to mean “reports will keep coming year after year.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and reports will keep coming year after year]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [that there is violence in the land, and that one ruler is fighting against another ruler]

47.note: Yahweh is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. See how you translated this phrase in 7:32 and 23:7. Alternate translation: [Therefore, pay attention, days are coming]

Yahweh is using **visit upon** as a common expression of the culture to mean that he is about to punish someone. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will come and punish] or [I will bring punishment on]

Here, **all of her land** represents “all of the people who live in her land.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and all of the people living in her land will be put to shame]

The expression **will be put to shame** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and I will put all of her land to shame]

48.q: וְ⁠רִנְּנ֤וּ עַל־בָּבֶל֙ שָׁמַ֣יִם וָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ וְ⁠כֹ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר בָּ⁠הֶ֑ם
48.note: Yahweh is speaking of **the heavens and the earth and all that is in them** as if they were living things that could **shout for joy**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the heavens and the earth will resound with the joyful shouts of all that is in them over Babylon]

Yahweh is referring to all of creation by naming its two major components, **the heavens** and **the earth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the whole created universe and everything in it]

This is the end of what Yahweh said, which began in verse 36. You may wish to mark the words of this speech with a first-level quotation mark at the beginning and end of them or with some other punctuation or convention that your language uses to indicate a first-level quotation.

49.q: גַּם בָּבֶ֕ל לִ⁠נְפֹּ֖ל חַֽלְלֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל גַּם לְ⁠בָבֶ֥ל נָפְל֖וּ חַֽלְלֵ֥י כָל הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ
49.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the people of other nations whom Babylon killed before the information about Babylon falling because of the people of Israel whom it killed. Alternate translation: [For Babylon, the slain of all the earth have fallen, so Babylon also is to fall for the slain of Israel]

49.q: גַּם לְ⁠בָבֶ֥ל נָפְל֖וּ חַֽלְלֵ֥י כָל הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ
49.note: Jeremiah says **all the earth** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [as also for Babylon the slain of countless peoples have fallen]

50.note: These commands are addressed to the people of Judah (the Israelites) who are living in Babylon, not to the people of Babylon. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You people of Judah who have escaped the sword, go]
Here, **the sword** represents “war.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Fugitives from the war]

Yahweh is using **Do not stand still** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Do not delay.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do not delay]

The implication is that the people of Judah are to keep worshiping Yahweh even while they are far away from their own land. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Continue to worship Yahweh even while you are far away from your land]

Yahweh is using **may Jerusalem come up on your heart** as a common expression of the culture to mean “may you think about Jerusalem.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and may Jerusalem be in your thoughts]

51.note: Here Jeremiah begins to quote what the people of Judah (the Israelites) say. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of the people of Judah or the Israelites. Alternate translation: [The people of Judah say, We are ashamed]

51.q: כִּֽי שָׁמַ֣עְנוּ חֶרְפָּ֔ה כִּסְּתָ֥ה כְלִמָּ֖ה פָּנֵ֑י⁠נוּ
51.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **reproach** and **disgrace**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [for we have heard how people scorn us; we look utterly humiliated]

Here the people of Judah are speaking as if **disgrace** were a covering that had spread over **our faces**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we are ashamed to show our faces] or [everyone sees us as disgraced]

51.q: כִּ֚י בָּ֣אוּ זָרִ֔ים עַֽל מִקְדְּשֵׁ֖י בֵּ֥ית יְהוָֽה
51.note: The implication is that when these foreigners entered the temple, they defiled the holy places there. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for strangers have defiled the holy places of the house of Yahweh by going into them]
See how you translated the similar expression in 17:26.

52.note: Yahweh is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Therefore, listen carefully, days are coming]

By **visit upon**, Yahweh means that he will carry out a judgment upon them, which in this case would be to destroy them. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers, as in the UST.

The implication is that **the slain** are people whom enemies have wounded so badly that they are dying. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and in all her land those whom enemies have mortally wounded will groan as they die]

53.q: כִּֽי תַעֲלֶ֤ה בָבֶל֙ הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֔יִם וְ⁠כִ֥י תְבַצֵּ֖ר מְר֣וֹם עֻזָּ֑⁠הּ מֵ⁠אִתִּ֗⁠י יָבֹ֧אוּ שֹׁדְדִ֛ים לָ֖⁠הּ
53.note: Here, **though** introduces the first part of a condition that could not actually happen. Yahweh is stating that even if Babylon could rise up to the heaves, he would still destroy it. Alternate translation: [Suppose Babylon could go up to the heavens, and suppose she could then fortify the height of her strength, even so from me destroyers would come to her]

Yahweh speaks of Babylon going up as high as **the heavens** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [Though Babylon should build itself up incredibly high]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [her strong high walls]

54.note: Here Jeremiah is expressing a strong feeling of alarm. There may be equivalent words or phrases in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [I hear the sound of]

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the destruction of Babylon were **a great breaking**, as when something is smashed to pieces. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and a great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans]
See how you translated the similar expression in 4:6.

55.note: Here, **the great voice** represents the loud noise of the crowds in the city as people come to buy and sell. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and he will put an end to her noisy commerce]

The pronoun **their** refers to those whose noise is like the roaring of water, referring to the destroyers who are coming against Babylon as described in verse 42. Alternate translation: [And the attackers as they come in waves will roar like many waters]

The point of this comparison is that just as **many waters** roar as they rush along, so the noise of the attacking armies will be loud and terrifying. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And their attacking armies will surge forward with a loud and terrifying noise, like floodwaters rushing along]

The expression **is given** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they send out the roaring of their voice]

56.note: Here the word **For** introduces an explanation for the previous statement: a roaring will be heard in Babylon because destroyers are coming there. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [This is because]

The expression **will be captured** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and enemies will capture her warriors]

Here, **their bows** represent the military power of the warriors of Babylon. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [their ability to fight will be destroyed]

Jeremiah is using the possessive form to describe a **God** who is characterized by **recompenses**, that is, a God who pays people back for what they have done. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [For Yahweh is a God who repays people for what they have done]

Jeremiah is repeating forms of the verb **repay** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [he will certainly repay in full]

57.q: וְ֠⁠הִשְׁכַּרְתִּי שָׂרֶ֨י⁠הָ וַ⁠חֲכָמֶ֜י⁠הָ פַּחוֹתֶ֤י⁠הָ וּ⁠סְגָנֶ֨י⁠הָ֙ וְ⁠גִבּוֹרֶ֔י⁠הָ
57.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if he would give the leaders of Babylon so much wine that he would **make them drunk**. It means that he will make them completely helpless. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this idea in Jeremiah 51:39. Alternate translation: [And I will take away from her officials and her wise men, her governors and her prefects and her warriors, all of their power]
See how you translated these same phrases in Jeremiah 51:39. Alternate translation: [and they will fall down like drunkards and die]

This phrase may have been spoken by Yahweh speaking of himself in the third person, or it may have been spoken by Jeremiah about Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person, as in the UST.

58.note: Here Yahweh is using the plural **walls** where he could have used the singular form. This suggests that he is using the plural form to emphasize the greatness of the wall that surrounded Babylon. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the singular and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [The massive wall of Babylon]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb in the expression **stripping bare, it will be stripped bare** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [will certainly be stripped completely bare]

The expression **it will be stripped bare** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [it will become completely bare]

58.q: וְ⁠יִֽגְע֨וּ עַמִּ֧ים בְּ⁠דֵי רִ֛יק וּ⁠לְאֻמִּ֥ים בְּ⁠דֵי אֵ֖שׁ
58.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if these people worked hard and were paid with **emptiness** and **fire**. This means that all of their work to build the city will come to nothing when enemies burn it all. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And all of the peoples’ labor will result in nothing; enemies will burn what they built]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **emptiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And the peoples will labor for what is worthless]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the communities will labor for fire]

59.q: הַ⁠דָּבָ֞ר אֲשֶׁר צִוָּ֣ה יִרְמְיָ֣הוּ הַ⁠נָּבִ֗יא אֶת שְׂרָיָ֣ה
59.note: Jeremiah is using this sentence to introduce a new prophecy, that is, the instruction that he gave to Seraiah, the official from the kingdom of Judah. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

59.q: אֶת שְׂרָיָ֣ה בֶן נֵרִיָּה֮ בֶּן מַחְסֵיָה֒
59.note: The words **Seraiah**, **Neriah**, and **Mahseiah** are the names of men.
The pronoun **he** refers to Seraiah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [when Seraiah went with Zedekiah]
See how you translated the similar expression in [39:1](ta:39).

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **fourth**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. See how you translated the similar expression in [25:1](ta:25). Alternate translation: [in year four of his reign]

Here Jeremiah is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. The ULT indicates this with the word **Now**. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

The expression **the officer of the resting place** refers to a royal official who arranged where the king would stay each night when traveling, along with other duties. If your readers would not be familiar with this kind of official, you could use the name of a similar official that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [was the king’s quartermaster]

60.q: אֵ֧ת כָּל הָ⁠רָעָ֛ה אֲשֶׁר תָּב֥וֹא אֶל בָּבֶ֖ל אֶל סֵ֣פֶר אֶחָ֑ד אֵ֚ת כָּל הַ⁠דְּבָרִ֣ים הָ⁠אֵ֔לֶּה הַ⁠כְּתֻבִ֖ים אֶל בָּבֶֽל
60.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **all these words that were written concerning Babylon** before the information about writing them **in one scroll**. Alternate translation: [all these words that were written concerning Babylon, that is, all the evil that would come to Babylon, in one scroll]

60.q: אֵ֧ת כָּל הָ⁠רָעָ֛ה אֲשֶׁר תָּב֥וֹא אֶל בָּבֶ֖ל
60.note: Here, **evil** represents disaster. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [about all of the disaster that would come to Babylon]

The phrase **all of these words** refers to everything that Jeremiah wrote in this book about what would happen to Babylon. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [all of these things that he had finished writing]

61.q: כְּ⁠בֹאֲ⁠ךָ֣ בָבֶ֔ל וְֽ⁠רָאִ֔יתָ וְֽ⁠קָרָ֔אתָ אֵ֥ת כָּל הַ⁠דְּבָרִ֖ים הָ⁠אֵֽלֶּה
61.note: The word **you** is singular here because Jeremiah is addressing Seraiah, so use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

61.q: וְֽ⁠רָאִ֔יתָ וְֽ⁠קָרָ֔אתָ אֵ֥ת כָּל הַ⁠דְּבָרִ֖ים הָ⁠אֵֽלֶּה
61.note: The implication is that Seraiah is to go to a public place in Babylon and read these words loudly so that the people in Babylon will hear them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [then you will make sure to find a good place to read all of these words out loud in the hearing of the people there]

The phrase **all of these words** refers to everything that Jeremiah wrote in the scroll that he gave to Seraiah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [everything in this scroll that I gave you]

62.note: What follows this instruction is what Seraiah is to pray to Yahweh. You could refer to this as a prayer if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [then pray out loud to Yahweh, saying,]

Jeremiah is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you have spoken** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it is Yahweh himself who has made these pronouncements against Babylon, and thus they will surely happen. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [you are the one who has spoken]

62.q: לְ⁠הַכְרִית֔⁠וֹ לְ⁠בִלְתִּ֤י הֱיֽוֹת בּ⁠וֹ֙ יוֹשֵׁ֔ב לְ⁠מֵ⁠אָדָ֖ם וְ⁠עַד בְּהֵמָ֑ה
62.note: Here, **to cut it off, to not be in it a dweller, to from man and to beast** summarizes the result of what Yahweh has spoken concerning Babylon. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the result of what Yahweh has said. Alternate translation: [that it will be cut off, that there will not be in it a dweller, not a man or a beast]

Jeremiah is using **to cut it off** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to destroy it.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to end it] or [to destroy it]

Jeremiah is referring to every living creature in the city by naming two extremes, **man** and **beast**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [with no living creature at all]

Here the word **for** introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [considering that]
If your language does not use nouns for the ideas of **desolations** and **perpetuity**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [a desolate place forever]

63.note: This phrase introduces further instructions. Use a natural way in your language to indicate that instructions continue after sentences that were not instructions. Alternate translation: [Then do this:]

64.note: Here Jeremiah is speaking as if the city of Babylon would **sink** like a stone in the river and never come up again. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Thus Babylon will be destroyed and will never recover]

Jeremiah is using **from the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of]
The pronoun **they** refers to the people of Babylon. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the people of Babylon will grow weary]

This phrase represents a word in the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. The phrase, however, does not seem to make sense in this place. Scholars have proposed that the prophecies originally ended with the phrase, **Until here are the words of Jeremiah**, at the end of verse 58, and the account of Seraiah’s mission in verses 59 to 64 was added later. At that time, a scribe may have accidentally included the word just before this final phrase when he moved it. For that reason, some modern translations leave it out in this place. You may want to follow the major translation in your area.

This sentence marks the end of the words that Jeremiah spoke and wrote concerning Babylon. Use the natural form in your language for expressing the conclusion of a story. Alternate translation: [This concludes the words of Jeremiah]
